Working notes: inventory ordering

- Costs: holding is small; stockout is ~1.00/unit and much worse. Ordering costs ~0.50/order. Bias toward avoiding stockouts.
- Lead time: orders placed today arrive in about 2 days. “Arriving over next 2 days” includes near-term arrivals; use it before ordering to avoid double-counting.
- Demand is volatile. Recent sales: 6, 4, 7, 7, 4, 3, 11, 1, 3. Average ~5/day, max 11. Two-day demand can reach ~22 without warning.
- Past mistake: underordering caused repeated stockouts, especially Days 5-7 and 9-10. Orders of 0-6 were too small once demand spiked. Stockout costs dominated daily cost.
- Policy: maintain inventory position (on hand + confirmed arrivals + on order) around 22-25 units. If position is below ~20, order enough to reach target. Do not order 0 when stock is 0 or incoming is below expected 2-day demand.
- If sales run high (>8/day), raise target toward 28-30. If sales cool (<4/day), lower target but keep above ~15 until variance is clearer.
- Ops notes (cycle count, temp worker, forklift, carrier pickup, racking) were noise. Counts matched system; no adjustments needed. Act only on count mismatch or explicit constraint.
- Review daily; because ordering cost is low, frequent small-to-medium orders are fine, but lead time means protection stock matters more.

Working notes: inventory ordering

- Costs: holding ≈0.10/unit/day, often main cost now. Ordering 0.50/order. Stockout ≈1.00/unit and worse; avoid stockouts, but don’t chase target daily.
- Lead time: orders today arrive in ~2 days. Check “arriving next 2 days” before ordering to avoid double-counting.
- Demand volatile. Recent 14 days: 3,11,1,3,7,2,3,5,3,7,4,7,4,12. Avg ≈5/day, max 12; 2-day demand can spike to ~19+.
- Lessons: early underordering caused stockouts, incl. Day 11 with 1 on hand. Later small top-ups when position was already 21–25 added holding/ordering costs without preventing stockouts. Day 19: position 21, order 0, cost 0.20. Day 20: 12-unit spike, position 9, ordered 21, no stockout.
- Policy: inventory position = on hand + confirmed arrivals + on order. Keep around 21–25, not always 25. Order only if position <20, or if sales >8 and position <25. If position 21–25 and demand normal, order 0. Do not order 0 if stock is 0 and 2-day arrivals are below expected 2-day demand. If sales cool <4, lower target toward 18–20; if high >8, raise toward 28–30. Avoid small top-ups; each order costs 0.50.
- Ops notes (temp receiving, racking, carrier pickup, cycle count) were noise unless count mismatch or explicit constraint. Counts matched.

Working notes: inventory ordering

- Costs: holding ~0.10/unit/day, ordering 0.50/order, stockout ~1.00/unit and worse. Stockouts are costly; don’t risk them for small holding/ordering savings.
- Lead time: orders today arrive in ~2 days. Check “arriving next 2 days” before ordering to avoid double-counting. Inventory position = on hand + confirmed arrivals + on order.
- Demand: recent 14 days: 4,7,4,12,3,6,6,7,6,8,4,8,8,8. Avg ≈6.5/day; max 12; 2-day demand often 12–16, can spike near 20. Demand is higher than earlier ~5/day.
- Lessons: Day 21 stockout (-3.00) despite position 27 because on hand was only 6 and no same-day arrival. Position can hide near-term shortage. Day 22 with 0 on hand and 21 arriving had no stockout. Days 23–30, small orders of 5–9 when position <20 kept stockouts at 0; costs were mostly 0.50 ordering, holding 0.00–0.80. Small top-ups can be justified if they protect against stockout.
- Policy: keep position around 22–26. Order if position <20. If sales >8, raise target toward 28–30 and order if position <26. If sales cool <4, lower target toward 18–20. Do not rely only on position: if on hand + today’s arrivals < expected next 1–2 days’ demand, order earlier/raise target. Avoid ordering 0 when on hand is 0 or very low and no same-day arrival.
- Ops notes: racking rotation, carrier pickup, temp receiving, cycle count were noise unless count mismatch or explicit constraint. Counts usually matched.
